The course content is not instructive, most of the papers we read are not suitable for undergraduate level. For example, why do we study Williamson in undergraduate? I looked at the Epistemology courses of many universities, for example NYU, they have two textbooks, as seen in their syllabus: Feldman's Epistemology and Rosenberg's Three Conversations about Knowing. Apart from that, there are papers they need to read some weeks. When they want to read names like Bonjour and Goldman, they allocate a week for the papers. No one expects these students to read Bonjour and Alston in a week and to summarize and criticize what Willamson explains in 34 pages in 800 words. So why does Jonathan expect this from us? Is there a single essay that satisfies him among the essays he has read? It is certain that there is not, anyway almost everyone got 15-22 out of 25. I guess this is a catalog course and no one will get an A. Anyway, I wouldn't give 25 out of 25 to someone who summarized and criticized Williamson in 800 words, it's not something that can be done. If there was something that could be done, I would not have studied at Bilkent and asked for a chair next to Williamson at Oxford. The only thing we read in class that we could easily understand was Gettier, which we read and passed in the first week. However, in the programs of many universities, they do not read Gettier in the first week. Let me give the example of NYU, they read Gettier in the 6th week, after going through the textbooks. In short, if you have studied epistemology before and do not want to take an undergraduate course, but want to take an epistemology course that can be given to graduate students, and if you want to deal with the challenge of expressing in 700-800 words what you normally need to express in 2000 words, it is definitely a good course, you can take it from Jonathan without thinking twice.
Sometimes the concepts would get hard to understand, and this is not an easy course by any means, but Jonathan's explanations would solve the problem.

course: There is no positive aspect to the course, it is a completely filler course. Under the name of political philosophy, we answer the question of what virtue is for a whole semester from different thinkers, some of whom are older than Jesus and we cannot even prove whether they were written by that person. The course teaches you how to copy and paste someone else's thought into your own words through these texts. The course is completely contrary to the nature of philosophy and producing original ideas.

instructor:
While the instructor is generally cheerful and well-intentioned, the lectures often feel more like listening to a monologue rather than an interactive class. At times, the instructor laughs unexpectedly during lectures, which can be distracting. Although I usually do not have difficulty concentrating in class, I personally struggled to maintain focus during these lectures. As a result, I found it challenging to respond to questions or actively participate, and I clearly observed that many of my classmates experienced similar difficulties.

The grading policy is quite strict. Additionally, the instructor is very unlikely to respond to emails, which makes communication outside of class difficult. However, when attending office hours, the instructor is helpful and willing to provide support.

The instructor taught the class by focusing on the important points of the philosophical texts and summarized the main points clearly. However, when we ask each other a question about a topic which the instructor explains, he acts aggressively and tells us to get out. I think it is not a good behavior for a professor.

course: Well philosophy of action is not everyone's cup of tea like many other things but even more so for this course. instructor: Even though the assigned material were all very hard to comprehend, the instructor made everything very clear during class hours. He was able to communicate all of these complex ideas very clearly and in a way that sparked interest.

He summarizes very heavy papers to-the-point and makes them easily understandable. His feedbacks on the essay assignments are very wisely guiding. He deems discussion-based classes significance. course: The course itself is so interesting and glad to take this course. It is related with the philosophy of mind and psychology topics as well as social and legal philosophy inquiries. As an implementation of the philosophy of action theories, it would be great is there were just a couple of papers showing these relations sincere there are not any courses in the Faculty indicating the applied side (in legal cases or empirical experiments) of philosophy of action.
Everything was great.
assistant: It would be good, if there was a TA of this course.

instructor: The strongest point of the instructor is that he is approachable. Additionally, he is excellent in guiding and giving feedbacks. However, one weakest point of the instructor is that he prefers in-class discussions more than lectures. In-class discussions have advantages and disadvantages. One of the disadvantages was that some discussions were out of topic and prevented getting into the main questions of the papers. In order to limit the scope of the discussions, he could have sent some guiding questions prior to each class. Alternatively, he could have short lectures before discussions. More of the short lectures or guiding questions could have hindered discussions being scattered. Given that this is an introductory course to Philosophy of Action, lectures could have worked more in presenting the already established debates in the literature.

Prof. Payton has a lot of wonderful qualities. His joyous disposition and respectful attitude toward the students and the students’ personal and academic processes are extremely encouraging. In terms of his teaching abilities, it is clear, from his ways of answering the questions by connecting philosophy of action to other disciplines in philosophy, that he knows his material: he has covered, when the need arose, stuff from metaphysics, language, and logic, among else. Bilkent is lucky to have him. In the future, when he inevitably becomes more and more famous in the field, I’ll count myself lucky to be able to say, “Ooh, Payton? I took a graduate course from him! And yes, — he’s as nice as the gossip makes him out to be.”

The instructor was very student-friendly, and stimulated interest in the subject. He was always energetic around the classroom which helped us focus on the topic more.
One downside was that I don't think he managed the time in-between the exams. For example, our second exam was assigned extremely close to our final exam date. But other than that, Jonathan is awesome!
P.S, his grading could be a whole lot better.
course: The strongest aspect of the course is that it gives a complete advanced introduction to the topic and incorporates most recent research in the syllabus. That being said, it might be better for Prof. Payton to start *every course* by covering the reading for the week for, like, 10-15 minutes and then wait for questions from the students. When he starts the course by asking if there are any questions, students might feel the urge to come up with ones, and when the students start by asking questions, the discussion goes to places that are sometimes irrelevant to the papers in hand. At least from my perspective, the discussions that immediately followed his lecturing at the beginning of the courses were more intellectually stimulating.

Strongest aspect: The material we read for this class was rather informative. I did learn a lot from this course. But most importantly, the in-class discussions were very helpful. So, because the class is based on discussions, it's important for your peers to contribute effectively.
Weakest aspect: It felt like the Intention chapter was too hard. The material for that aspect of the course was more than the other sections. The readings were harder, and less interesting, in my opinion.
